source.title: Rogue Scalpel: Activation steering breaks refusal, even with benign directions

record.tranche_reason: The post uses activation steering and reports unintended harmful compliance from steering with random, SAE, and language-related directions. It does not test the specific harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or the claim versions’ stated interventions.
record.gate_note: The post also reports feature counts and prompt-level generalization for its steering experiments; those are included as outcomes below. Its discussion of the original single refusal direction is background, not a result from this study.
record.test_reason: The post steers with random vectors, SAE features and language difference-in-means directions, then measures harmful compliance. It never extracts, ablates or adds the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and makes no weight edit. The refusal-direction paper is cited as background. The post argues that its effects are not explained by closeness to that direction, but the argument uses a random-geometry estimate, not a measured projection. No result bears directly on any version. It does not use the refusal direction as a tool, so T4 and uses_without_test are wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that steering, even with random or benign directions, can unpredictably bypass refusal. They hold that this is not simply overlap with the refusal direction and urge checking for side effects. Effect sizes vary by model, and only open-weight models up to 70B were tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation addition with random, SAE, and language-related directions and measures harmful compliance; it does not ablate the claimed harmful-minus-harmless direction across layers and positions or add that direction to test harmless-request refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported effects vary by model; for the Llama-3.1-8B difference-in-means results, compliance varies by language.

fits_no_version.finding: Random Gaussian steering raises harmful compliance from 0% to 2-27% depending on the model. 387 of 1000 random directions break at least 5 of 100 prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering residual activations with random directions degrades refusal in open-weight chat models.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features raise compliance 2-4 pp above random vectors. 353 of 1000 features break at least 5 prompts, and the top feature breaks 35. Effective features include benign concepts such as 'Portugal'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering with benign SAE features can unintentionally bypass refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Features that break one prompt rarely break prompts in other categories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which steering vector bypasses refusal is prompt-specific and hard to predict.

fits_no_version.finding: Language difference-in-means steering on Llama-3.1-8B gives 0.9-12.4% compliance, varying by language.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept steering with difference-in-means vectors degrades refusal to a degree that depends on the concept.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors argue that refusal breaking by random directions is not explained by alignment with the refusal direction. The argument uses a cosine-distribution estimate, not measured projections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal degradation from steering is not mediated solely by overlap with the refusal direction.

record.problems: The post gives only a range across models for random-vector steering and does not provide model-specific values. Several outcomes are qualitative, uncertainty estimates are not reported, and the general-capability effects are not evaluated.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and no capability evaluation.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the refusal direction, and no adversarial training.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction refusal representations. That many unrelated directions degrade refusal is a different construct.
The language directions are language-concept steering vectors, not a refusal direction transferred across languages.

missing.what: 387/1000 random directions break at least 5 of 100 prompts, the count the authors compare against SAE features.
missing.locator: It's not just the refusal direction

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong summary of arXiv:2509.22067; the full paper may contain projection analyses absent here. Relation changed from uses_without_test/T4 to discusses/T6: the refusal direction is neither used nor tested. The rows lack per-model values.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation of the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, no addition of that direction to induce harmless-request refusal, and no general-capability evaluation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or of training against its ablation.
The post does not test whether refusal is represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
The post reports language-conditioned steering outcomes, but does not test transfer of the same refusal direction across languages, model variants, or training stages.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or timing.
